title: A Little Thanks Goes a Long Way
text:
In 2010 Adam Grant and Francesca Gino published four studies on why being thanked makes people more willing to help. Most were laboratory experiments in which students who had given feedback on a cover letter were then asked for more help. Those who had received a short note of thanks were far more likely to help again.

The final study took place in a university fundraising call center. Callers there phoned alumni to request donations, and their calls were tracked by the center's system. One day, the director of annual giving visited one group of callers and told them she was very grateful for their hard work and contributions to the university. A second group did not receive the visit.

During the following week, the callers who had been thanked made more than 50 percent more calls than before, while the other group's number of calls stayed about the same. In the lab studies, the researchers found the main reason: being thanked made people feel socially valued, which in turn made them willing to give more of themselves.
lesson: A sincere thank you costs nothing and tells people their effort is seen. Make it a habit, and say specifically what you value.
location: A US university fundraising call center
source: Grant, A. M., and Gino, F. (2010). A little thanks goes a long way: Explaining why gratitude expressions motivate prosocial behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 98(6), 946-955.
caveat: Francesca Gino was later found by Harvard to have falsified data in other papers; this paper was not among those retracted, but its results deserve some care.
